subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.stage_label: Observe and broaden the concept of health
periods.activity_description: Students examine the case study from Activity 3.1 — a student experiencing social isolation and excessive screen time — and record what physical, mental, and social symptoms emerge. They then compare this against the WHO definition of health and the Ayurvedic perspective to surface the three-dimensional nature of health.

roles.role_description: Presents the Activity 3.1 case study and guides students to notice symptoms across physical, mental, and social dimensions.
Records observations from the case study, then compares them to the WHO and Ayurvedic definitions of health.

materials: Printed or projected text of Activity 3.1 case study
Blank observation grid (three columns: Physical / Mental / Social)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Activity 3.1 case study aloud; students note any health-related details they notice in the student's story.
Students individually list all the symptoms they identified and sort them into physical, mental, and social columns in a quick observation grid.
Teacher introduces the WHO definition and the Ayurvedic view of health; students annotate their grid to match each symptom to a dimension.
Class shares findings and together articulates why the case-study student is not fully healthy even without a named disease.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit sets the chapter's conceptual anchor: health is not merely the absence of disease. A common starting misconception is that a person who is not visibly ill must be healthy — the Activity 3.1 case study is designed to disrupt this directly, so resist the urge to explain before students have recorded their own observations. If students list only physical symptoms, ask them to re-read the social details of the case study as a checkpoint before moving to the WHO definition.

periods.stage_label: Observe and broaden the concept of health
periods.activity_description: Students carry out Activity 3.2 by generating a personal list of good and harmful habits, then work in pairs to sort the habits by which dimension of health each affects. They also examine the two playground images from Activity 3.3 to recognise that environmental conditions belong on the same map.

roles.role_description: Generates a personal habit list and independently sorts habits into health-promoting or health-harming categories.
Discusses the habit list with a partner and together places each habit on a shared habits-to-dimensions map that also includes the environmental observations from Activity 3.3.
Circulates to prompt thinking about why environmental cleanliness belongs on the same map as personal habits.

materials: Activity 3.2 habit-list worksheet
Printed or projected clean and polluted playground images from Activity 3.3
Blank habits-to-dimensions map template

time_bands.activity: Each student writes a personal list of good and harmful habits from their daily life without consulting peers.
Pairs compare lists and collaboratively create a habits-to-dimensions map, placing each habit under the health dimension it primarily affects.
Teacher displays the two playground images from Activity 3.3; pairs annotate their map with an 'environment' row, recording what risks the polluted playground introduces and why the AQI matters.
Pairs share one surprising placement from their map with the class, and the teacher consolidates that environment is an equal contributor to health alongside personal habits.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established the three dimensions of health conceptually; this unit grounds them in students' own habits and surroundings. Watch for the misconception that a clean personal lifestyle is sufficient for good health — the polluted playground images are the key tool to challenge this, so give pairs adequate time to annotate the environment row before consolidating. If students struggle to distinguish which dimension a habit affects, prompt them to ask: 'Whose body, whose mind, or whose relationships does this harm?'

periods.stage_label: Classify diseases by cause and transmission
periods.activity_description: Students are given a set of disease cards (each naming a disease, its causal agent, and how it spreads) drawn from the examples in Sections 3.4 and 3.4.1. They classify each disease as communicable or non-communicable and then further sort the communicable diseases by their route of transmission, justifying each placement.

roles.role_description: Reads each disease card, decides on a classification, and arranges cards into a two-level sort on the desk — first by communicable/non-communicable, then by transmission route.
Poses probing questions when groups hesitate — particularly about whether asthma or diabetes could be 'caught' — and draws the class together to compare classifications.

materials: Disease classification cards (one per disease from Table 3.1 plus NCDs from Section 3.4.2)
Two-level sort mat

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly connects to the previous unit by noting that some health threats come from within our habits and some from outside our bodies via pathogens, then introduces the term 'pathogen' and distributes disease cards.
Groups sort the disease cards into communicable and non-communicable piles, writing one-sentence justifications for each card.
Groups further sort the communicable pile into transmission-route subcategories — airborne, waterborne/foodborne, vector-borne, direct contact — again recording justifications.
Groups compare their final sorts and resolve disagreements; teacher consolidates the two-level classification on the board using the chapter's examples.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves from observing health broadly to classifying disease systematically — the shift from stage one to stage two. A persistent misconception is that any serious disease must be communicable; watch for students placing cancer or diabetes in the airborne category. Prompt them to ask: 'Can you catch this from someone?' as a quick classification check before they commit a card to the communicable pile.

periods.stage_label: Classify diseases by cause and transmission
periods.activity_description: Students complete Activity 3.4's Table 3.1, filling in causal agent, site of infection, symptoms, and preventive measures for communicable diseases already sorted in the previous unit. They then extend the table with a parallel NCD section, populating it with lifestyle-related and deficiency causes from Section 3.4.2.

roles.role_description: Completes both sections of the extended Table 3.1 using the chapter text, comparing entries across the group to check consistency.
Models how to read Table 3.1 for one disease, then circulates to ensure students are recording causal agents accurately rather than just symptoms.

materials: Extended Table 3.1 worksheet (communicable + NCD sections)
Chapter text (Sections 3.4, 3.4.1, 3.4.2)

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the previous unit's two-level sort and shows how each card's information maps onto the columns of Table 3.1, modelling one entry together.
Groups complete Table 3.1 for all communicable diseases in their transmission-route categories, using the chapter text to fill in causal agent, site of infection, symptoms, and preventive measures.
Groups add an NCD section to the table, recording at least three NCDs with their non-pathogen causes — lifestyle, diet, deficiency, or environment — and one preventive or management measure each.
Each group cross-checks one another's NCD rows for accuracy; teacher highlights any common errors, particularly around deficiency diseases being classified as communicable.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit gave students the classification framework; this unit fills it with evidence from the text. A frequent error is leaving the 'causal agent' column blank for NCDs on the assumption that only pathogens count as causes — prompt students to write 'nutrient deficiency' or 'lifestyle factor' explicitly in that column. Remind groups that the NCD section will be needed in the next unit, when they move from classifying to explaining why these diseases arise.

periods.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms of spread and prevention
periods.activity_description: Students trace the causal chain from pathogen entry through immune response to vaccine-acquired immunity, using Jenner's smallpox investigation as a worked scientific example. They construct a cause-and-effect flow diagram connecting transmission route, infection site, immune response, and vaccine action.

roles.role_description: Guides students through Jenner's observation, hypothesis, and experiment, making explicit how each step in the scientific method connects to the mechanism of immunity.
Constructs a flow diagram during the explanation, adding each causal link as it is discussed rather than copying a completed version.

periods.activity_title: Why Pathogens Spread — and How the Body Fights Back
materials: Blank flow diagram template (pathogen → transmission → infection site → immune response → vaccine action)
Projected or printed 'Think like a scientist' Jenner sequence from chapter

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the completed Table 3.1 by asking: now that we know how diseases are classified, how does the body resist them — and when it fails, what helps? This frames immunity and vaccines as the next causal layer.
Teacher narrates Jenner's 'Think like a scientist' sequence — observation, hypothesis, inoculation experiment, global eradication — while students add each causal step to a personal flow diagram.
Teacher explains the mechanism of vaccine action: weakened or dead pathogen parts train the immune system to produce acquired immunity; students extend their diagram to show this pathway.
Students compare their completed flow diagrams with a neighbour and identify one step they had placed in the wrong sequence, then correct it.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous two units classified diseases; this unit asks students to explain the mechanisms that cause spread and that prevent it — a genuine step up in cognitive demand. A common confusion here is that vaccines cure disease rather than prevent it; the distinction between 'acquired immunity before exposure' and 'treatment after infection' should be made explicit during the Jenner narrative. Ask students to identify the moment in Jenner's sequence when prevention rather than treatment became the goal, as a checkpoint before moving on.

periods.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms of spread and prevention
periods.activity_description: Students analyse the Activity 3.7 infographic on how antibiotic resistance develops and, using the mechanism of antibiotic action described in Section 3.5.1, infer what behaviours accelerate resistance and what precautions slow it. They record inferences in an evidence-reasoning-conclusion format.

roles.role_description: Examines the infographic, constructs evidence-reasoning-conclusion entries for at least two behaviours that accelerate resistance, and proposes at least one precaution with a mechanistic justification.
Prompts groups to ground each inference in the mechanism — why antibiotics target bacterial structures absent in human cells — rather than simply listing do's and don'ts.

materials: Printed or projected Activity 3.7 infographic on antibiotic resistance
Evidence-reasoning-conclusion chart template

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the previous unit's immunity flow diagram by noting that when immunity and vaccines are not enough, treatment is needed — and introduces the discovery of penicillin as the parallel 'Think like a scientist' example.
Groups study the Activity 3.7 infographic and list the stages at which resistance develops, identifying what is happening to the bacterial population at each stage.

Each group completes an evidence-reasoning-conclusion chart: evidence from the infographic, reasoning grounded in how antibiotics work, and a conclusion about which human behaviour drives each stage of resistance.
Groups share their top precaution and its mechanistic justification; the class together identifies which precautions address resistance at the population level versus the individual level.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established the immune and vaccine mechanism; this unit extends causal reasoning to what happens when those defences fail and treatment is introduced improperly. Students often confuse antibiotic resistance as meaning the person becomes resistant, rather than the bacteria — the infographic's population-level view is the key tool for correcting this, so push groups to describe what happens to the bacterial population at each stage. In the next unit, students will apply all of this causal understanding to novel prevention scenarios, so the quality of mechanistic reasoning here is the preparation.

periods.stage_label: Apply integrated understanding to distinguish, prevent, and manage disease holistically
periods.activity_description: Students are presented with the Bhadrak district sanitation case study from Activity 3.6 and a second contrasting scenario involving a community with rising diabetes and dengue rates. For each scenario they apply the full chapter's framework — holistic health dimensions, disease classification, transmission mechanism, immune defence, and treatment limits — to recommend a prevention and management strategy with causal justification.

roles.role_description: Analyses each community scenario, identifies the diseases present, classifies them, traces their causal mechanisms, and produces a written prevention-and-management recommendation grounded in all chapter concepts.
Prompts groups to ensure their recommendation addresses all three health dimensions and distinguishes between communicable and non-communicable strategies, then facilitates a cross-group comparison.

periods.activity_title: Designing a Prevention Strategy for a Given Community Scenario
materials: Printed Activity 3.6 Bhadrak case study text
Contrasting community scenario card (diabetes and dengue rates rising)
Structured recommendation template

time_bands.activity: Teacher frames this unit as the place where all previous work converges: the three-dimensional view of health, the two-category disease classification, the causal mechanisms of spread and immunity, and the limits of treatment all bear on real community decisions.

Groups analyse the Bhadrak case study and the contrasting diabetes-and-dengue scenario, applying the classification and causal mechanism knowledge from units three through six to identify why each disease is present and how it spreads or develops.

Groups write a structured prevention-and-management recommendation for each scenario, explicitly distinguishing communicable from non-communicable strategies and identifying which health dimensions each measure addresses.

Two groups share contrasting recommendations and the class evaluates whether each recommendation is grounded in causal reasoning or merely in general advice, with the teacher highlighting where the holistic health lens makes the strategy stronger.

periods.teacher_notes: All previous units have built toward this moment — students are asked to synthesise the holistic definition of health, the disease classification, causal mechanisms, and prevention logic into a recommendation for a novel scenario. Watch for groups who treat dengue and diabetes identically, applying the same strategy to both; the evaluation criterion is whether they distinguish between vector-borne communicable prevention and lifestyle-driven NCD management. The Bhadrak case study is the chapter's own worked example of community-level prevention, so ask groups to name one principle from Bhadrak that does or does not transfer to the diabetes-and-dengue scenario.
homework: Survey two or three adults in your home about a lifestyle-related health condition they know of in the neighbourhood; for each condition, identify whether it is communicable or non-communicable, name its likely cause, and suggest one prevention measure — bring your findings as a written paragraph.

Using the chapter's immunity and antibiotic sections, explain in writing why a doctor might advise completing a full course of antibiotics even after you feel better — connect your explanation to what happens to the bacterial population if the course is stopped early.

periods.stage_label: Apply integrated understanding to distinguish, prevent, and manage disease holistically

roles.role_description: Analyse assigned scenarios, construct written recommendations that draw on the full conceptual arc of the chapter — health dimensions, disease type, transmission or cause, immunity or treatment mechanism, and prevention strategy — and present their reasoning to the class.
Frames the synthesis task, circulates to probe reasoning at each conceptual layer, and leads a closing discussion that draws the full chapter together under the dissolution test's central claim.

periods.activity_description: Students receive a one-page dossier about a fictional coastal fishing village — Neelavur — that contains a hand-drawn map, an AQI reading strip, a short list of reported illnesses from the village health worker's register, a food-habit summary, and three villager quotes describing how they feel day-to-day. Working in groups, students build a 'health file' for Neelavur by annotating the dossier: classifying each illness, tracing each causal pathway, identifying which health dimensions are under threat and why, and recommending targeted actions that distinguish communicable from non-communicable responses. Groups then rotate to critique one another's files before a whole-class convergence that names — through the work itself — the chapter's central ideas.
periods.activity_title: The Coastal Village Health File: Reading a Place Through the Whole Chapter
materials: One printed Neelavur dossier per group of four (see visual aid: 'Neelavur Dossier')
One annotation framework card per group (see visual aid: 'Annotation Framework Card')
Blank A4 sheets, two per group, for the health file write-up
Coloured pens or pencils, at least two colours per group — one for communicable, one for non-communicable
Blackboard or whiteboard and chalk or markers for the closing convergence list

visual_aids.title: Neelavur Dossier
visual_aids.text:
NEELAVUR — COASTAL FISHING VILLAGE HEALTH DOSSIER

MAP ELEMENTS (hand-drawn or printed):
Show a river, fishing docks, houses, a fish-drying ground close to houses, one health sub-centre, and the notation: 'AQI: 148 — Unhealthy for sensitive groups'.

VILLAGE HEALTH WORKER'S ILLNESS REGISTER EXCERPT:
Six conditions reported: cholera, dengue, Type 2 diabetes, tuberculosis, anaemia, skin infections.

FOOD-HABIT SUMMARY:
Most families eat fish daily; rice and vegetables twice a day; packaged snack consumption has risen in the past two years; drinking water drawn from river.

VILLAGER QUOTES:
Quote 1 (fisherman, adult): 'I feel tired all the time even when I am not sick.'
Quote 2 (mother): 'My child was never vaccinated — the health worker came but we were at sea.'
Quote 3 (teenager): 'I have no friends here; I stay inside and eat chips most of the day.'

visual_aids.title: Annotation Framework Card
visual_aids.text:
TASK A — For each illness in the register, write whether it is communicable or non-communicable and name its causal agent or factor.

TASK B — For communicable illnesses, trace the transmission route using evidence from the map and food-habit summary.

TASK C — For each villager quote, identify which health dimension(s) — physical, mental, social — is affected and why.

TASK D — Write two targeted actions for Neelavur that distinguish what you would do differently for communicable diseases versus NCDs, and state which prevention tool (hygiene, vaccine, lifestyle change, environmental improvement) each action uses.

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes the Neelavur dossier face-down and the annotation framework card face-up. Without explaining the dossier, teacher says: 'Neelavur is a coastal fishing village. A health worker has handed you everything she knows about it — a map, an illness register, a food summary, and three things villagers told her. Your job is to build a health file for this village using everything you have studied.' Students turn the dossier over and read it in their groups without writing. Teacher then fields only factual clarifications about the dossier's content — no conceptual hints.

Groups work through Tasks A and B on the annotation framework card. They mark each illness in the register as communicable or non-communicable in one colour and write the causal agent or factor beside it. For communicable diseases they draw an arrow on the map or write a sentence tracing the transmission route — for example, connecting 'river water for drinking' to cholera, or 'fish-drying ground near houses' and 'standing water' to dengue. Teacher circulates, asking groups who finish Task A quickly: 'How do you know tuberculosis spreads differently from cholera — what does the map tell you?' and prompting groups who are uncertain about anaemia: 'Is there a pathogen involved, or is something missing from the diet?'

Groups move to Tasks C and D. For Task C they annotate each villager quote — the tired fisherman triggers discussion of whether tiredness alone makes someone unwell and which dimension of health is affected; the unvaccinated child connects to acquired immunity; the isolated teenager surfaces the social and mental dimensions and the link between lifestyle and NCD risk. For Task D groups write their two targeted actions, explicitly labelling each with its prevention tool. Teacher listens for groups that write the same action for cholera and diabetes ('eat healthy food') and prompts: 'Would eating healthy food stop cholera spreading through the river water? What would — and which chapter concept is that?'

Groups swap health files with one adjacent group. Each group reads the file they have received and writes two critique comments on a blank sheet: one thing the file got right with a reason, and one gap or error — for example, a file that traces dengue transmission correctly but recommends only antibiotics for it, or one that addresses physical health in all three quotes but misses the social dimension in the teenager's quote. Teacher gives groups two minutes to read and two minutes to write their critique, then each group returns the file and verbally delivers its critique to the authoring group in one minute.

Teacher draws a vertical line on the board creating two columns — left blank, right headed 'What the task needed'. Addressing the whole class: 'Tell me one thing you had to know to complete any part of this task.' As students name concepts — the three dimensions of health, communicable versus non-communicable, transmission routes, what a vaccine does, what a symptom versus a sign is, what a pathogen is, why lifestyle matters, what the AQI means — teacher writes each on the right side. When the list is complete, teacher draws a bracket around it and says: 'This list is the chapter. You just used it all at once on a village none of us had seen before — that is what the chapter is for.' No further summary is given.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit asks groups to build a 'health file' for the fictional coastal village of Neelavur by annotating a multi-part dossier, deliberately designed so every chapter concept — the three dimensions of health, communicable vs NCD classification, transmission routes, immunity, and prevention tools — surfaces through new, unfamiliar terrain. Do not pre-explain the dossier; let the annotation framework card guide groups, and during the closing band resist summarising yourself: ask 'What did you need to know to do this task?' and build the chapter map from student answers. Full dossier content and the annotation framework tasks are in the prepared materials (see material).

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and broaden the concept of health
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students examine a case study and a personal habits map to recognise that health encompasses physical, mental, and social dimensions shaped by both lifestyle and environment.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify and sort observable physical, mental, and social indicators of health from a case study or personal example, and explain why a person without a named disease may still not be fully healthy.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify diseases by cause and transmission
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students sort disease cards into communicable and non-communicable categories with transmission-route sub-classification, then complete a full disease profile table with causal agents, sites, symptoms, and preventive measures.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify a given disease as communicable or non-communicable with a justified reason, and for communicable diseases specify the transmission route and causal agent using the chapter's examples.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms of spread and prevention
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct a cause-and-effect flow diagram of immunity and vaccination using Jenner's investigation, then infer from the antibiotic resistance infographic how specific human behaviours drive or reduce resistance.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can trace the causal chain from pathogen transmission to immune response and vaccine-acquired immunity, and explain with mechanistic reasoning why incomplete antibiotic use accelerates bacterial resistance.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Apply integrated understanding to distinguish, prevent, and manage disease holistically
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students apply the full chapter framework — holistic health, disease classification, transmission mechanisms, immune defence, and treatment limits — to analyse community scenarios and produce causally justified prevention and management recommendations.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can distinguish communicable from non-communicable diseases in an unfamiliar scenario and produce a prevention or management strategy that addresses lifestyle, environmental, and biological factors with explicit causal justification.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and broaden the concept of health
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify and sort observable physical, mental, and social indicators of health from a case study or personal example, and explain why a person without a named disease may still not be fully healthy.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: A student sleeps well, eats nutritious food, and has no diagnosed disease, but avoids spending time with classmates and feels lonely most days. According to the WHO definition of health discussed in the chapter, which statement best describes this student's health?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is fully healthy because no disease has been diagnosed.

options.label: B
options.text: The student is not fully healthy because eating nutritious food without exercise is harmful.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is not fully healthy because sleep and food cannot maintain health without medicine.

options.label: D
options.text: The student is not fully healthy because social well-being is missing even without a diagnosed disease.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student holds the chapter's target misconception — that health equals absence of disease — and has not applied the WHO three-dimensional definition.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses health with medical treatment dependency, importing an external idea not grounded in the chapter's framework.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student conflates two lifestyle habits (diet and exercise) in a way that misrepresents the chapter's content; the option is a plausible-sounding but inaccurate chapter detail.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with abstract definitions can anchor their answer in the Activity 3.1 case study's concrete symptoms. Students who express their answer verbally before marking can articulate which dimension is missing.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and broaden the concept of health
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify and sort observable physical, mental, and social indicators of health from a case study or personal example, and explain why a person without a named disease may still not be fully healthy.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes an Ayurvedic view of health that includes dinacharya and ritucharya. What does this perspective add to the WHO definition of health?

options.label: A
options.text: It adds the idea that health can only be maintained through modern medicines and vaccines.

options.label: B
options.text: It adds the idea that health requires balance of body, mind, and surroundings through daily and seasonal routines.

options.label: C
options.text: It adds the idea that physical fitness alone is sufficient for complete health.

options.label: D
options.text: It replaces the social dimension of health with the environmental dimension only.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses Ayurveda's traditional scope with the biomedical model, failing to distinguish the two frameworks presented in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has partially read the Ayurvedic description and incorrectly concluded it removes a WHO dimension rather than expanding the framework.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has regressed to the narrow physical-only view of health that the chapter explicitly challenges.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students unfamiliar with Ayurvedic terminology can locate dinacharya and ritucharya in Section 3.1 and use the context to answer. Students who prefer a visual mode can sketch the three-way balance (body, mind, surroundings) before selecting.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify diseases by cause and transmission
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given disease as communicable or non-communicable with a justified reason, and for communicable diseases specify the transmission route and causal agent using the chapter's examples.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: A child develops goitre. A classmate develops malaria. Which row correctly classifies each disease and gives its cause?

options.label: A
options.text: Goitre — communicable, caused by a pathogen; Malaria — non-communicable, caused by poor diet.

options.label: B
options.text: Goitre — communicable, spread by direct contact; Malaria — non-communicable, caused by hormone imbalance.

options.label: C
options.text: Goitre — non-communicable, caused by a virus; Malaria — communicable, spread by contaminated water.

options.label: D
options.text: Goitre — non-communicable, caused by iodine deficiency; Malaria — communicable, spread by mosquito vector.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has reversed the classification of both diseases, likely conflating 'deficiency' with 'infectious' and applying the communicable label to any illness that sounds medical.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student correctly identifies goitre as non-communicable but assigns a viral cause, confusing it with a communicable disease mechanism; for malaria, the student has mis-assigned the transmission route from Table 3.1.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has swapped the classification of both diseases and assigned the hormone-imbalance cause (from diabetes in the chapter) to malaria, indicating cross-contamination between NCD examples.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can refer to their completed Table 3.1 from the classification unit as a reference tool. Students who benefit from articulating reasoning can explain their classification aloud to a partner before marking.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify diseases by cause and transmission
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify a given disease as communicable or non-communicable with a justified reason, and for communicable diseases specify the transmission route and causal agent using the chapter's examples.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Disease | Causal Agent | Transmission Route
Tuberculosis | Bacteria | ?
Cholera | Bacteria | ?
Dengue | Virus | ?
Diabetes | Lifestyle/hormonal | ?
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. A student is completing a disease profile table. Which row has the transmission route correctly filled in for all four diseases?

options.label: A
options.text: Tuberculosis — airborne; Cholera — airborne; Dengue — contaminated water; Diabetes — no person-to-person transmission.

options.label: B
options.text: Tuberculosis — airborne; Cholera — contaminated water/food; Dengue — mosquito vector; Diabetes — no person-to-person transmission.

options.label: C
options.text: Tuberculosis — contaminated water; Cholera — airborne; Dengue — direct contact; Diabetes — vector-borne.

options.label: D
options.text: Tuberculosis — direct contact; Cholera — contaminated water/food; Dengue — mosquito vector; Diabetes — airborne.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused the transmission routes of tuberculosis and cholera, likely misremembering which bacterial disease is airborne and which is waterborne from Table 3.1.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student correctly places tuberculosis as airborne but then incorrectly applies airborne transmission to cholera and waterborne to dengue — a systematic mis-sorting of the three subcategories.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student assigns direct contact to tuberculosis, confusing it with diseases such as chickenpox, and assigns airborne transmission to diabetes, failing to recognise it as a non-communicable disease.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can use the chapter's Table 3.1 groupings (airborne, waterborne/foodborne, vector-borne) as a three-category scaffold before reading the options. Students who process information sequentially can check one disease at a time against each option.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: Ascariasis is listed in the chapter as a foodborne communicable disease. State the type of causal agent responsible, name the transmission route, and identify one preventive measure that directly addresses this route.
expected_elements: Causal agent is a worm (parasite/helminth) — not a bacterium or virus.
Transmission route is contaminated food or water.
Preventive measure directly addresses the route — e.g., washing food, ensuring clean drinking water, or handwashing before eating.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who recall the causal agent type but not its technical name (helminth) may write 'intestinal worm' — this is acceptable and equivalent. Students who prefer to draw can sketch the transmission chain (contaminated food → ingestion → infection) alongside their written answer.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain causal mechanisms of spread and prevention
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can trace the causal chain from pathogen transmission to immune response and vaccine-acquired immunity, and explain with mechanistic reasoning why incomplete antibiotic use accelerates bacterial resistance.

competency.competency_text: Explain the effect of nutrition and lifestyle on health.

assessment_items.question_text: Edward Jenner observed that milkmaids who had cowpox did not get smallpox. He then inoculated a boy with cowpox material and exposed him to smallpox. Which statement best explains the mechanism by which this experiment protected the boy?

options.label: A
options.text: The cowpox exposure killed the smallpox pathogen directly before it could enter the boy's bloodstream.

options.label: B
options.text: The cowpox exposure trained the immune system to recognise a related pathogen, producing acquired immunity before smallpox exposure.

options.label: C
options.text: The cowpox material cured any smallpox infection already present in the boy's body at the time of inoculation.

options.label: D
options.text: The cowpox material strengthened the boy's physical health generally, making all diseases less likely to take hold.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student confuses vaccine function with antibiotic function — applying the curative model to what is a preventive mechanism, which is the chapter's explicit distinction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student holds a vague general-strengthening model of immunity rather than the specific acquired-immunity mechanism explained through Jenner's experiment.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student conflates the immune system's action on pathogens with direct destruction by the vaccine material itself, missing the trained-recognition step.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who built a flow diagram during the immunity unit can trace the pathway from inoculation to acquired immunity on that diagram before selecting. Students who prefer verbal reasoning can narrate the sequence aloud before committing to an answer.

assessment_items.question_text: A patient stops taking antibiotics after three days because they feel better, even though the prescribed course is seven days. Using the mechanism of antibiotic resistance explained in the chapter, what is the most likely consequence at the population level of the bacteria?

options.label: A
options.text: Stopping the antibiotic early has no effect on the bacterial population as long as symptoms have disappeared.

options.label: B
options.text: The bacteria that survive become less harmful because the antibiotic has weakened them permanently.

options.label: C
options.text: The surviving bacteria — those most resistant to the antibiotic — multiply and pass on resistance, making the infection harder to treat.

options.label: D
options.text: The surviving bacteria quickly die without antibiotic pressure because the immune system eliminates them fully.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student assumes the immune system will finish what antibiotics started, not recognising from the infographic that resistant bacteria survive specifically because they are not cleared by either mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses 'surviving bacteria' with 'weakened bacteria', misreading the chapter's population-level resistance mechanism as an individual-level weakening.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student equates symptom disappearance with bacterial elimination, which is the exact misconception the chapter's antibiotic section addresses.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can revisit the Activity 3.7 infographic stages and map each stage to the patient's three-day versus seven-day scenario before selecting. Students who need a visual anchor can draw a simple before-and-after population diagram of bacteria.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that antibiotics are effective against bacteria but not against viruses or protozoa. Using the mechanism described in Section 3.5.1, explain why this is the case and give one example from the chapter of a disease for which antibiotics would therefore be ineffective.
expected_elements: Antibiotics work by targeting bacterial cell structures that are absent in human cells.
Viruses and protozoa do not have the same bacterial cell structures, so antibiotics have no target to act on.
A named example of a viral or protozoan disease from the chapter — e.g., dengue (viral), influenza (viral), malaria (protozoan) — for which antibiotics would be ineffective.

assessment_items.question_text: A public health officer visits a village where many adults have diabetes and many children have cholera. She has a limited budget for intervention. Which combination of interventions is best justified by the chapter's framework for preventing and controlling disease?

options.label: A
options.text: Distribute antibiotics to all residents for both conditions, since antibiotics address the bacterial cause of both diseases.

options.label: B
options.text: Focus only on cholera using improved sanitation, since NCDs like diabetes are not preventable through community action.

options.label: C
options.text: Promote lifestyle changes (diet and physical activity) for diabetes management, and improve water and food sanitation to interrupt cholera transmission.

options.label: D
options.text: Vaccinate all residents against both diabetes and cholera, as vaccines are the most effective prevention tool described in the chapter.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student over-applies the vaccine solution from the immunity section without recognising that vaccines target specific communicable pathogens and that no vaccine for diabetes is described in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student applies antibiotics to diabetes — an NCD — demonstrating a failure to distinguish communicable from non-communicable disease management mechanisms.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly identifies the sanitation strategy for cholera but fails to apply the chapter's NCD prevention framework, which explicitly includes lifestyle changes as a community-level tool.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can use their completed disease profile table to check the causal mechanism of each disease before evaluating the options. Students who prefer to think through options verbally can narrate the justification for each intervention before selecting.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes the Bhadrak sanitation campaign as an example of disease prevention. Which feature of the campaign best illustrates the chapter's principle that prevention is preferable to cure?

options.label: A
options.text: The campaign distributed antibiotics to all community members as a precaution before any illness was reported.

options.label: B
options.text: The campaign improved personal nutrition to strengthen individual immune systems against waterborne pathogens.

options.label: C
options.text: The campaign reduced open defecation before cases of diarrhoea and infection occurred, removing the transmission route rather than treating established illness.

options.label: D
options.text: The campaign trained community members to identify symptoms of illness so they could seek treatment faster.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student confuses preventive with curative pharmaceutical intervention, applying the antibiotic model to a sanitation campaign that operates at the environmental level.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student conflates prevention with early detection — symptom identification enables faster treatment but does not prevent the disease, which is the chapter's explicit distinction.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly identifies nutrition as a health factor but misapplies it to the Bhadrak case, which the chapter describes as a sanitation and environmental intervention, not a nutritional one.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can re-read the Bhadrak case study text from Activity 3.6 before selecting. Students who need scaffolding can first identify what the campaign did and then check whether that action removed a transmission route or treated existing illness.

assessment_items.question_text: A school in an urban area has high rates of both dengue (a communicable disease) and Type 2 diabetes (a non-communicable disease) among its students. The school principal asks for a single coordinated health plan that addresses both conditions. Using the chapter's framework for how diseases arise, spread, and can be prevented or managed, construct a health plan for this school. Your plan must: (1) explain the causal mechanism of each disease; (2) distinguish why different strategies are needed for each; and (3) propose at least one prevention or management measure for each disease with a causal justification grounded in the chapter.
look_for: Clear statement of dengue's causal mechanism — viral pathogen spread by mosquito vector — contrasted with diabetes's non-pathogen cause — lifestyle, diet, physical inactivity, hormonal factors.
Explicit recognition that communicable and non-communicable diseases require distinct strategies: vector control and hygiene for dengue; lifestyle modification and early diagnosis for diabetes.
At least one dengue prevention measure causally connected to interrupting the transmission route — e.g., eliminating mosquito breeding sites or using protective clothing.
At least one diabetes prevention or management measure causally connected to its NCD cause — e.g., increasing physical activity, reducing processed food intake, or early glucose monitoring.
Integration of the holistic health framework: the plan acknowledges at least one social or environmental dimension (not just individual behaviour) in addressing either disease.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find the open-ended structure challenging can use their completed disease profile table as a scaffold, extracting the causal agent, transmission route, and prevention columns for each disease before writing the plan. Students who prefer structured formats can write two labelled sections — one for dengue and one for diabetes — before integrating them with a shared environmental dimension.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Health problem reported | Likely disease type | Causal mechanism | Prevention or management strategy | Which health dimension(s) addressed
A family drinks water from an open well near a waste dump site | Severe diarrhoea in children | | | |
A teenager spends 8 hours daily on screens, rarely exercises, eats mostly packaged food | Fatigue, weight gain, borderline high blood sugar | | | |
A factory neighbourhood has heavy vehicle and industrial smoke | Frequent respiratory illness in residents | | | |
A community stopped vaccinating children after rumours spread | Outbreak of measles reported | | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. Four community scenarios are described. For each scenario: (1) identify whether the health problem is most likely communicable or non-communicable and state the likely disease type; (2) explain the causal mechanism — what is causing or transmitting the problem; (3) propose one prevention or management strategy grounded in the chapter's content; and (4) identify which dimension(s) of health — physical, mental, or social — the problem affects.
assessment_items.scaffold: Work through each scenario row by row. For the disease type, ask: can this be passed from one person to another through a pathogen? For the causal mechanism, ask: what in this scenario is causing or spreading the problem — a pathogen, a lifestyle factor, an environmental factor, or a failed prevention system? For the strategy, choose one that directly addresses the mechanism you identified. For the health dimension, remember the WHO definition: physical, mental, and social well-being are all part of health.
format_of_output: Completed table with all five columns filled for each of the four scenarios.
A short written paragraph (three to four sentences) explaining which two scenarios you found most different from each other and why — focusing on why their strategies cannot be swapped.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires students to distinguish communicable from non-communicable diseases in unfamiliar scenarios and produce causally justified prevention strategies across lifestyle, environmental, and biological factors — a classification-with-justification task is the most direct demonstration vehicle for this integrated operation.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates the student's ability to apply the chapter's full analytical framework — holistic health, disease classification, causal mechanisms, and prevention logic — simultaneously across four contrasting unfamiliar scenarios, and to articulate why different disease types require different strategies.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold's two questions — 'can this be passed from one person to another?' and 'what in this scenario is causing the problem?' — operationalise the communicable/non-communicable distinction and the causal mechanism step. The written paragraph at the end is the integrative demonstration: it requires students to reason across scenarios rather than process each one in isolation. Weak responses will complete the table but produce a paragraph that merely summarises rather than contrasts.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses name the specific causal mechanism for each scenario (e.g., waterborne bacterial transmission, not just 'dirty water'), propose a strategy directly tied to that mechanism (e.g., improving well cover and treating water, not just 'be hygienic'), cover all three health dimensions across the four scenarios, and write a paragraph that explains why swapping the strategies of two contrasting scenarios would fail. Weak responses use vague causal language ('bad habits', 'germs'), apply the same generic strategy (e.g., 'stay clean') to multiple scenarios, and write a paragraph that restates scenario descriptions rather than reasoning about mechanism differences.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find all four scenarios challenging simultaneously can complete the two communicable scenarios first, then the two non-communicable ones, before writing the comparative paragraph. Students who process information visually can colour-code rows by disease type before filling in the mechanism and strategy columns. The scaffold questions are designed to be usable by students who have the knowledge but need a processing sequence to organise it.

result.section_coverage_note: Every section is covered; the closing sitting draws the chapter together in one synthesis.
